summary: This experimental document specifies how DTLS can protect RADIUS traffic. Plain RADIUS has limited authentication and encryption and depends on fixed shared secrets, so using DTLS gives stronger security.

eli5.summary: The old way of sending login messages is like using a postcard with a simple lock. This RFC puts them in a sealed, locked envelope so no one can read or copy them.

questions: what port does radius dtls use
subtitle: RADIUS keeps its packet format but travels inside DTLS, trading fixed shared secrets for real transport security.

tldr.problem: RADIUS over UDP sends data in the clear, relies on MD5-based checks, lets attackers replay packets, and authenticates peers with fixed shared secrets.
tldr.mechanism: Each RADIUS packet is handed unchanged to a DTLS layer on UDP port 2083, and servers track DTLS sessions by 4-tuple with rules for opening, idling and closing them.
tldr.outcome: RADIUS/DTLS is Experimental, and RFC 9765 has since updated it. RADIUS/UDP is not recommended for long-term use outside isolated and secure networks.

today: RFC 7360 is an Experimental RFC and has been updated by RFC 9765. The RFC itself leaves open whether it would advance to Standards Track, depending on real-world uptake.

sections.title: The Problem with RADIUS over UDP
sections.content:
RADIUS has traditionally used MD5-based methods for per-packet authentication and integrity checks. MD5 has known weaknesses, so some specifications recommended IPsec. The RFC finds IPsec awkward because the RADIUS application cannot control or monitor the network security policy, since it is implicit in the network configuration.

This specification instead uses DTLS (RFC 6347) as a RADIUS transport. The application can monitor and control the security policy, and RADIUS stays UDP-based. It does not fix everything: DTLS adds no reliable or in-order delivery and does not fragment application messages, so RADIUS/DTLS shares those issues with traditional RADIUS.

The document is Experimental. The authors note open questions such as whether pre-shared keys or X.509 certificates will prevail, and that it was not yet decided whether the approach would go to Standards Track.
sections.eli5: The old way was a postcard with a weak lock. The new way keeps the same message but puts it in a strong sealed envelope.

sections.title: What Changes and What Stays the Same
sections.content:
The RADIUS packet format is unchanged. So are the permitted codes, the Request and Response Authenticator calculations, the length limits, attribute formats and the obfuscation of attributes such as User-Password. The application builds a RADIUS packet as usual and passes it to DTLS instead of a UDP socket. Implementations MUST support encapsulated RADIUS packets of 4096 octets.

Only two things change. Length checks use the length of the decrypted DTLS data rather than the UDP length, and extra octets past the Length field are ignored as padding. The shared secret used for the MD5 integrity checks and attribute encryption MUST be the fixed string radius/dtls.

Most of the RADIUS/TLS specification (RFC 6614) applies, read with TCP replaced by UDP and TLS by DTLS. Client identities SHOULD come from DTLS parameters rather than only the source IP address.
sections.eli5: The letter inside the envelope is written exactly the same way as before. Only the envelope is new.

sections.title: Ports and Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
The default destination port is UDP/2083, with no separate ports for authentication, accounting and dynamic authorization. Everything arriving on that port MUST be treated as DTLS, and RADIUS/UDP MUST NOT be accepted there. Servers MUST NOT accept DTLS on the old RADIUS/UDP ports, and they MUST authenticate clients. Clients MUST authenticate with credentials unique to each client.

RADIUS has no protocol negotiation, so moving to DTLS is an out-of-band administrator decision. Clients SHOULD NOT probe for DTLS support, and if a server configured for DTLS seems unresponsive the client MUST NOT fall back to RADIUS/UDP but treat the server as down. A server that serves a client on several ports MUST keep a per-client "DTLS Required" flag, and silently discards non-DTLS packets from such a client. Allowing both RADIUS/UDP and RADIUS/DTLS from one client is NOT RECOMMENDED because it exposes traffic to downgrade attacks.

It is RECOMMENDED that both sides support TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, which give perfect forward secrecy.
sections.eli5: Everything that comes to the special mailbox must be in a sealed envelope. If the sealed way is not working, you may not fall back to a postcard.

sections.title: Session Management
sections.content:
TCP is not there to track sessions, so servers track DTLS sessions by a 4-tuple: source IP address, source port, destination IP address and destination port. Each entry holds the DTLS session, an optional Last Traffic timestamp and implementation data. A server MUST NOT retransmit an old DTLS packet. It caches the RADIUS response and sends it through DTLS again to make a new packet.

Because attackers can forge UDP, servers SHOULD use the stateless cookie technique from RFC 6347 and MUST limit partial sessions. Sessions MUST be deleted on a TLS closure alert, a fatal alert, a malformed packet, a bad Message-Authenticator or Request Authenticator, or non-RADIUS traffic. A well-formed but unexpected RADIUS packet SHOULD NOT cause deletion, to leave room for future extensions.

Idle sessions SHOULD be deleted after a configurable idle timeout that SHOULD NOT be below 60 seconds or above 600 seconds. A server MUST ignore attempts to reuse the 4-tuple of an active session. Clients SHOULD use DTLS Heartbeats and the Status-Server watchdog (RFC 3539, RFC 5997) and close sessions that are idle for three watchdog timeouts.
sections.eli5: The server keeps a list of open conversations and hangs up on any that go quiet too long or try tricks. A newcomer cannot hijack an existing conversation just by pretending to be at the same address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using DTLS largely mitigates RADIUS encryption and authorization weaknesses, but not issues in the unchanged packet format. The fixed secret radius/dtls is acceptable only when DTLS uses non-null encryption, so null encryption MUST NOT be used. A legacy RADIUS/UDP shared secret MUST NOT be reused for DTLS, and implementations must not quietly turn it into a TLS-PSK key. PSK keys SHOULD come from a CSPRNG, must be at least 16 octets, and SHOULD be 32 octets or longer.

Instead of shared secrets, TLS credentials MUST be used by each party to authenticate the other. Clients SHOULD start with an empty list of trusted CAs rather than the public CAs that browsers carry, because a public CA would let any server with a certificate from it see all the RADIUS traffic, including user credentials. Servers MUST limit the number of tracked and partially open sessions. Clients behind a NAT must use TLS or DTLS and be uniquely identifiable.
sections.eli5: Do not reuse the old password for the new lock, and only trust key-makers you picked yourself, not every one in the world.
